questions.question: Why can't you make a synchronous callout directly from a trigger?
options: Triggers don't have access to the Http class
Callouts are blocked during a transaction with pending DML, and triggers run inside that transaction
It's allowed, but only for SOAP, not REST
There's no such restriction
questions.explanation: This is a core governor rule; triggers must hand the callout off to an async context like Queueable or @future(callout=true).

questions.question: What is a key limitation of @future methods compared to Queueable Apex?
options: @future methods can make unlimited callouts
@future methods always run synchronously
@future methods can't easily chain into further async work or accept complex parameter types like sObjects
@future methods can only be called from Batch Apex
questions.explanation: @future methods take simple parameter types and are fire-and-forget; Queueable supports complex parameters and job chaining.

questions.question: Why is making one callout per record risky inside a Batch Apex execute() scope of 2,000 records?
options: Batch Apex doesn't support callouts at all
It has no risk as long as Database.AllowsCallouts is implemented
Governor limits don't apply inside Batch Apex
It can easily exceed the 100-callouts-per-transaction limit, since that limit applies per batch scope
questions.explanation: Callout limits are enforced per transaction; a 2,000-record scope making one callout each would blow past the 100-callout ceiling. Shrink the scope size when each record needs a callout.

questions.question: What's the danger of chaining Queueable jobs without a bound?
options: There is no danger, Queueable chaining has no limits at all
It can build an effectively unbounded loop of jobs if there's no stopping condition
Chained Queueable jobs automatically cancel themselves after 10 chains
Chaining is disabled by default and must be explicitly turned on
questions.explanation: Queueable chaining is powerful for bounded pipelines but dangerous if used to build an open-ended loop — design a stopping condition.

questions.question: Why is "wrap it in try/catch and move on" not a complete strategy for async Apex error handling?
options: try/catch blocks are not supported in asynchronous Apex
Async Apex never throws exceptions
Salesforce automatically emails all users on any async failure
Async failures are invisible to the end user by default, so a swallowed exception means nobody finds out
questions.explanation: Async jobs run outside any user's direct view — pair error handling with logging or alerting so failures surface instead of disappearing silently.
